title: Network-hosted PowerShell execution with destructive script behavior
purpose: Define evidence-backed requirements for the Week 5 Windows Sigma candidate and executable Janus JSON detection rule.

implemented_chain: Assumed Kali foothold establishes RDP access to the Windows client
The Windows client performs PowerShell host and domain discovery
The Windows client uses WinRM to prove approved access to the domain controller
An approved payload is staged on the NETLOGON share
The Windows client starts a separate PowerShell process that executes the network-hosted simulated wiper
The simulated wiper deletes only approved dummy files
scenario.primary_detection_target: Observable PowerShell execution and destructive script behavior on the Windows client
not_claimed: The domain controller remotely launches the Windows client process
The simulation reproduces a complete historical intrusion
The Week 4 specification is an implemented detection

in_scope: PowerShell Event ID 4103 module or pipeline content
Behavioral comparison of development baseline and attack runs
One backend-neutral Sigma candidate in Week 5
One executable Janus Windows JSON rule in Week 5
Local evaluation against schema-valid windows_events.jsonl evidence
out_of_scope: Sysmon Event IDs other than 1 in version one
Direct Sigma execution against normalized evidence

held_out_validation.selection_policy: Use the highest-numbered clean attack run and highest-numbered clean baseline run unless an evidence-quality defect is documented before analysis.

evidence_split.reuse_policy: If the rule is revised after holdout evaluation, those holdout runs become development data and may not be described as unseen again.

future_correlation_enhancements: Preserve PowerShell process_id when supplied by event XML
Preserve PowerShell script_block_id, runspace_id and script_path when supplied
Retain user SID and account name separately when both are available

A_network_hosted_powershell_execution.condition: all AND at least one any_suspicious_context condition

medium_confidence: Component A matches without a correlated Component B
Component B matches without a correlated Component A
correlation.high_confidence: Components A and B occur on the same host within five minutes.

correlation_quality.requirement: Same host and same process ID within five minutes
Same host and compatible normalized user identity within five minutes

correlation_quality.limitation: May combine unrelated administrative activity and must be marked as lower-quality correlation.

correlation.reason: Sysmon and PowerShell may represent the same user as an account name and a SID respectively.

expected_attack_result.with_4103_or_4104: High-confidence alert when Components A and B correlate.
expected_attack_result.without_4103_or_4104: Medium-confidence alert from Component A; the absence of PowerShell content must be reported.
required_alert_evidence: References to contributing normalized and raw records
Explanation that uses only allowed features

expected_baseline_result.handling: Record and investigate every baseline match as a potential false positive; do not conceal or discard it.

likely_cases: Approved administration scripts executed from network shares
Backup or maintenance tooling that removes temporary files
PowerShell automation using noninteractive or execution-policy options
controls: Do not alert on PowerShell execution alone
Require a generic network-hosted path plus suspicious execution context for Component A
Use destructive content as a separate component rather than treating every script block as malicious
Compare component frequency and combinations against development baseline runs
Document environment-specific exclusions only after evidence-backed validation
Do not globally allowlist PowerShell, administrators, UNC paths or NETLOGON

sigma_candidate.purpose: Portable detection of Component A using canonical Windows/Sysmon fields

janus_windows_json_candidate.purpose: Executable local representation of Components A and B, correlation and alert output
janus_windows_json_candidate.deployment: Copy an approved, schema-valid rule into the Janus controller active-rules location

generation_requirements: One retry after invalid structured output, followed by documented manual correction if necessary
API key read from an environment variable and excluded from prompts, output and logs

development_phase: Generate and tune only with the two assigned attack and two assigned baseline runs
Record every medium- and high-confidence alert
Record observed baseline false positives and missed attack behavior
Freeze the Sigma and Janus JSON candidates before holdout access
holdout_phase: Evaluate once against the assigned one attack and one baseline holdout
Record whether the held-out attack triggered and at what confidence
Preserve matched evidence references and evaluator output
Do not claim general accuracy from the small lab sample
acceptance_requirements: The held-out attack produces at least one medium- or high-confidence alert without prohibited identifiers
Every alert traces back to normalized and raw evidence
Baseline outcomes and false positives are reported without concealment
Missing PowerShell telemetry causes an explicit degraded-confidence result rather than fabricated evidence
Results are described as lab-observed validation outcomes

current_actions: Write a Windows Application Event Viewer warning and display a BurntToast notification
Attach a valid observed RDP source IP when available
Mark attribution unresolved when no valid source is observed
safe_response_candidate.pfsense_role: The required Week 6 pfSense block is OT-triggered. IT-triggered containment remains a future stretch item.

known_limitations: PowerShell 4103 and 4104 depend on logging configuration and may be absent.
Sysmon Event ID 1 proves process creation but not destructive impact by itself.
Generic UNC execution and PowerShell cleanup commands can be legitimate.
Host-and-time fallback correlation may join unrelated events.
Current PowerShell normalization may not expose a process ID for strong cross-source correlation.
RDP attribution identifies an observed source connection but does not prove intent or causation.
The wiper log and before-and-after file inventories are experimental ground truth, not production detection inputs.
The small controlled dataset supports lab validation only and cannot establish production accuracy.
Sigma correlation behavior varies by backend; the Janus JSON rule is the executable local detection artifact.

approval.change_control: After approval, changes require a new version and documented reason.
